claim: NASA's fire-protection technical brief says that on Earth smoke detectors sit on the ceiling because smoke travels upward, but in space smoke does not rise, so detectors are placed within the ventilation system.
quote: On Earth, smoke detectors are installed on the ceiling or upper section of a wall because that's the direction in which smoke travels. In space, smoke doesn't rise, so detectors are placed within the ventilation system.
source_title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Fire Protection (OCHMO-TB-008, Rev A)
source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (OCHMO)
source_org: NASA OCHMO
locator: PDF p. 2, section 'Overview' (paragraph beginning 'Detecting a fire in space is also different')
limits: A reference brief derived from NASA-STD-3001, not an experiment: it states a design rule but gives no detection times and no test data. It states the rule in general terms; a NASA operations paper (Tobias and McMillan 2020, SpaceOps) says ISS cabin smoke detectors are 'either located out in the open cabin, or within cabin air ducting', so not every ISS detector sits in the ducts. Describes crewed vehicles such as the ISS; partial gravity (Moon, Mars) is not covered by this sentence.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found, PDF p. 2). Claim reworded to attribute the rule to the brief instead of saying NASA puts all detectors in ducts, because the SpaceOps 2020 paper (also in this file) says ISS cabin detectors are either in the open cabin or in the air ducting.

claim: In the roughly 20 years of Space Shuttle operations that the paper has just described, only five potential fire-causing incidents (component overheating or electrical short circuits) occurred, and in none of them was the early fire signal strong enough to make a smoke detector go off.
quote: In the same period, only five potential fire-causing incidents of component overheating or electrical short circuits occurred. In no case was the incipient-fire signature strong enough to cause a smoke detector to actuate
source_title: Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions (NASA/TM-2000-210337, AIAA 2000-5251)
source_authors: Robert Friedman, David L. Urban
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center
locator: section 'False Alarms' (the preceding sentence gives '20 years of Shuttle operations'; the quote starts at 'In the same period')
limits: Covers Shuttle experience up to about 2000, not the ISS. The sentence continues across a column break (the crew recognised and corrected the problem); that continuation is not part of the verified quote. The paper does not say where the detectors were relative to each overheating component, so it shows these events were too weak or too far to trip a detector, not that a detector could never see them.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found). The '20 years of Shuttle operations' comes from the sentence just before the quote (there is a footnote marker '14' between the two sentences, so it cannot be put inside one clean quote); claim now says so instead of implying the quote contains it. NTRS record: NASA/TM-2000-210337, September 2000, Friedman and Urban, Glenn. 'Recorded' changed to 'occurred' to match the text.

claim: Spacecraft life-support designers keep the cabin air well mixed, and a NASA Glenn review says this mixing dilutes smoke so that, in most cases, the whole vehicle volume must reach the alarm threshold instead of smoke collecting in a thin layer at the ceiling.
quote: This mixing dilutes the smoke such that, in most cases, the entire vehicle volume must be brought up to the alarm threshold rather than smoke collecting in a thin layer at the ceiling

conditions.flow_text: cabin ventilation keeps the open volume well mixed

limits: A NASA review paper that summarises modelling of smoke transport (cited as Brooker et al. 2007 and Urban et al. 2016), not a measurement in a real spacecraft fire. In lunar gravity buoyancy returns and the paper says design choices would differ.

quote: Of particular concern is the fact that these systems may not remove hazardous products as they remove particles. The net result is accumulation of hazardous compounds while alarm triggering is delayed

source_authors: Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban, Daniel L. Dietrich

limits: Model-based conclusion (lumped-element and CFD smoke-transport models of overheating spacecraft materials), not an in-flight measurement of a real fire. Whether it happens depends on vehicle volume, mixing rate, filtration rate and the alarm threshold chosen.

claim: In one Saffire VI test of a burning plastic (PMMA) slab inside an uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft, the smoke was readily detected, but the far-field detector reached a typical alarm threshold (1 mg/m3, which the authors call a relatively tight one) only at 981 seconds on the test timeline, by which time most of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
quote: The smoke from the fire event was readily detected by an ionization detector and a light scattering system but a typical alarm threshold was only achieved at 981 seconds. By this time most of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
source_title: Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment (ICES-2024-365)
source_authors: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff, Paul Ferkul, John Easton, Michael Johnston, Jay Owens, Sandra Olson, Claire Fortenberry et al.
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center with NASA Johnson Space Center and international partners

conditions.flow_text: 20 cm/s concurrent air flow over the sample in the Saffire flow unit; vehicle air mixed by fans

limits: Preliminary results for ONE test (VI-3, two-sided PMMA), burned at reduced pressure (54.6 kPa) and raised oxygen (30.3%), not normal ISS air. The 1 mg/m3 alarm level was chosen by the authors; the detector was a terrestrial ionization unit in the far-field unit near the hatch, not the ISS detector. 981 s is read off the experiment time axis, not time since ignition, and the paper does not state the delay after ignition. The body text says 'much of' the hazardous gas release had occurred by then; the conclusion says 'most'. Smoke particles were partly lost to surfaces on the way.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found; it is in the Conclusion, PDF p. 6). Dropped 'large fire test': the same paper calls these 1.5-3 kW fires 'a small fire by terrestrial standards'. Made explicit that the threshold was the authors' choice and that the smoke WAS detected, only late. Reading Fig. 4 on PDF p. 5, the igniter current switches on at roughly 650 s on the 'Time (s)' axis, so the delay after ignition is shorter than 981 s; I did not put this in the claim because the paper does not state it and Fig. 7 is labelled 'Elapsed Time (s)'. Table 1 values for VI-3 (54.6 kPa, 30.3% O2, 16.7 m3) confirmed from the rendered page.

claim: A NASA Johnson ISS materials manager listed it as a conundrum in 2001: detecting a fire needs air flow to carry smoke to the sensor, yet air flow is the worst thing for a microgravity fire.
quote: Solve conundrum of o Air flow needed for to transport smoke, combustion products to traditional sensors for fire detection o Air flow worst thing for microgravity fires
source_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety: A Human Space Flight Program Perspective (workshop slides, in NASA/CP-2003-212103)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center (ISS Materials and Processes Manager)
locator: slide 13 of 14, 'FIRE DETECTION' (the 'o' marks are the slide's sub-bullets; the original has the typo 'needed for to transport')
limits: A 2001 workshop slide stating an engineer's judgement, with no data behind it. Later Saffire tests (2020-2021) show the picture is more nuanced: very low air flow can also keep some fires alive and let fuel vapour build up.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found, PDF p. 7 = slide 13 of 14). The 'o' characters inside the quote are the slide's bullet glyphs and 'needed for to transport' is the original typo, so show the quote with ellipsis or bullets, not as flowing prose. Source is NASA/CP-2003-212103 (published April 2003) for a workshop held 25-26 June 2001; slide dated June 2001; Pedley is ISS Materials and Processes Manager at JSC. Claim is worded as what the slide lists, not as a measured fact. Note the same slide says 'No true fires on orbit, excepting SFOG, combustion experiments'.

claim: A NASA Glenn researcher (lead author Marit Meyer), quoted by NIST, said the ISS light-scattering smoke detector easily picked up large smoke particles but frequently failed to detect the smaller particles from Teflon and Kapton, which are extensively used in electronics, 'the most likely source of fire and smoke in space'.
quote: However, it frequently failed to detect the smaller smoke particles from Teflon and Kapton, a big concern because both materials are extensively used in electronics which is the most likely source of fire and smoke in space.

source_org: NIST (secondary source; quotes NASA Glenn)

conditions.fuel: Teflon, Kapton, cellulose, silicone rubber, Pyrell heated below ignition to make smoke

limits: SECONDARY source: a NIST news article quoting the paper's lead author; the Fire Safety Journal paper itself is paywalled and was not opened. The test heated samples to make smoke in a glovebox (no flame, no whole-cabin transport). 'Frequently' is not quantified in the article.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found; NIST news release of 1 May 2018). Original claim said the MATERIALS are the most likely source; in the quote the phrase refers to electronics ('both materials are extensively used in electronics which is the most likely source of fire and smoke in space'). Reworded and attributed to the NASA researcher via NIST. Secondary source (NIST, a federal agency, quoting NASA Glenn); the Fire Safety Journal paper (doi 10.1016/j.firesaf.2018.04.004) was not opened. 'Frequently' is not quantified.

claim: The published conclusion of the ISS smoke experiments is that the smoke particles were not significantly different from those made in equivalent tests in normal gravity, yet the two spacecraft detectors still did not detect every type of smoke.
quote: Results from the ISS experiment show that smoke particles vary in morphology and average diameter, however, they are not significantly different from smoke particles generated in equivalent experiments performed in normal gravity. The two spacecraft smoke detectors did not successfully detect every type of smoke
source_title: Evaluation of Spacecraft Smoke Detector Performance in the Low-Gravity Environment (Fire Safety Journal 98, abstract hosted by NIST)
source_authors: Jiann C. Yang, Thomas G. Cleary, Marit Meyer, David L. Urban, George W. Mulholland, Victoria Bryg, Zeng-guang Yuan, Gary A. Ruff
source_org: NIST / NASA Glenn (journal abstract)

conditions.fuel: five common spacecraft materials heated (oxidative pyrolysis)

limits: Abstract only (full paper paywalled, not opened). It means particle size and shape were not the main gravity effect in these tests. The earlier SAME hypothesis (larger smoke particles in microgravity) is therefore not what makes detection hard; the delay comes from how smoke is transported, mixed and filtered (see other claims). Smoke from heated samples, not a flaming fire.
story_use: what we still do not know
verifier_note: Quote re-checked (found) against the NIST publication page, which reproduces the abstract. Author list on that page: Yang, Cleary, Meyer, Urban, Mulholland, Bryg, Yuan, Ruff (the NIST news release lists Meyer as lead author of the same paper), so source_authors is correct. This claim is an important counterweight: it should stop the story saying that microgravity smoke is a different kind of smoke.

claim: A NASA computer model of a fire in a sealed, ISS-Destiny-sized cabin found that under-ventilated fires (excess fuel relative to the air reaching them) give high levels of carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen fluoride, while the levels are much lower for fuel-limited fires.
quote: For under-ventilated fires where there is an excess of fuel relative to oxidizer (cabin air flowrate to the fire) the analysis shows high levels of carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen fluoride. The levels of these contaminant species are much lower for fuel-limited fires.
source_title: Determination of Realistic Fire Scenarios in Spacecraft
source_authors: Daniel L. Dietrich, Gary A. Ruff, David L. Urban
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center
locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); discussion in section III.C 'Contaminant Species' (PDF p. 7), where the paper notes that in microgravity there is no buoyant mixing and a typical fire response is to turn ventilation off, so the whole cabin volume cannot be assumed to feed the fire. Year from the NTRS record (2013); the paper itself shows no date

conditions.pressure_text: sealed cabin of 65 cubic metres at 1 atm in the model (ISS Destiny-sized)
conditions.fuel: PMMA monomer, and a PMMA/Teflon mixture for the fluorine case

limits: A chemical-equilibrium COMPUTER MODEL, not a measurement; the authors say the equilibrium calculation 'is likely inaccurate' because large-scale reduced-gravity fire data are lacking. The contaminant result comes from prescribed masses of PMMA monomer (and a 75% PMMA / 25% PTFE mix for hydrogen fluoride) reacting in 1 to 15 cubic metres of air, not from a time-resolved fire. The paper's other main example (about 200 kW fire, pressure relief valve) is a very large fire, far bigger than the small, quiet fires of the Saffire tests.

quote: The trace contaminant control fire on Mir showed that carbon monoxide, which can be generated in large quantities from a small fire, can cause serious effects on crew health.

source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (OCHMO)

limits: A lessons-learned summary with no measured CO level. The brief does not say outright that the 'trace contaminant control fire' is the 24 February 1997 oxygen-generator fire described in the bullet above it, although both sit under the 'Mir (1997)' heading. The same page says it 'caused little damage and no injuries', while ICES-2020-173 says the 1997 event 'involved burns to the crewmember fighting the fire'.

claim: A NASA operations paper says that when the ISS fire alarm sounds, fans are automatically switched off and oxygen generation and gas introduction are stopped, with the design aim of stopping air and oxygen flowing toward the fire so that it can burn itself out.
quote: Intramodular and intermodular fans are deactivated, gas introduction is terminated, oxygen generation systems are deactivated, and location specific fans are deactivated, all performed in order to stop flowing air/oxygen towards the combustion event. This should eliminate local airflow, removing the Oxygen leg of the fire triangle and allowing the event to burn itself out.

source_authors: Barry Tobias, Courtenay McMillan

limits: Describes the design intent ('should eliminate local airflow'), not a measured outcome. limits: One test of one thin, charring fuel (cotton jersey, 50 cm long, 40 cm wide) at raised oxygen (26.2%) and reduced pressure (70.7 kPa), so it burns more readily than in normal cabin air. Both small flamelets and glowing char embers were seen 10 s after the flow stopped, and the authors say they cannot tell which one kept the fabric burning, though a surviving flamelet is judged likely. The paper's text gives about 280 s for fan-off and also says the fabric burned steadily for 300 s with the fan on.

Original claim said the fabric 'survived' 70 seconds, which suggests the visible flame carried on; the source says only that the flame grew back when flow returned and that flamelets and embers were both present, so wording was made neutral and the limits spell it out. Sample width (40 cm), 26.2% O2 and 70.7 kPa confirmed from the abstract and Table 1 of the paper.
